children: New York City is considering new ways to regulate the artificial intelligence industry, and the city council has called on representatives from OpenAI
to attend a special hearing on October 5, according to the
Council speaker Julie Menin sent letters to the companies on Tuesday, citing "a recent wave of alarming reports exposing the potential for AI to cause unparalleled cataclysmic harm."

"We're talking about companies that are bringing up the end of humanity as a possible outcome of this technology," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, according to the report. "And it has been a very flip response to that level of concern."

Mamdami supports legislation being pursued by U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders (D-Vt.) and U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), which calls for a nationwide moratorium on new data centers or upgrading existing ones.

"Specifically, no AI data center may be constructed or upgraded until laws are enacted (1) subjecting AI products to prerelease federal review and approval for safety and effectiveness, and (2) ensuring that AI-related economic gains benefit workers and the people of the United States (including by preventing AI-related job loss)," according to the bill summary.
However, Mamdami does not believe this proposed bill goes far enough.

"What are the federal government's policies to ensure that this rapidly advancing technology is going to be regulated, as opposed to just simply determined through a profit motive, or through the decisions of a few individualized companies that will or will not have an IPO sometime soon?" he said.

It's unknown what potential regulations the NYC City Council could enact on AI applications or even how they could potentially regulate the advanced software. However, the NYC Department of Education did enact limits on AI tools across its school system. It prevents most students from using AI in a school setting until at least high school.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the state's RAISE act, the Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, last December. It allows the state to impose a $1M fine on companies that don't report critical safety issues related to frontier AI models within the first 72 hours of an event. Subsequent violations call for $3M fines. It goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Hochul also enacted a one-year moratorium on all new data centers in the state using 50 MW or more of power on July 14.
